strengths: The paper targets an important practical limitation of frame-aggregated detection metrics: autonomous-driving reliability depends strongly on range and environmental conditions, and a distance-conditioned metric could be useful for system design.
The controlled clear-versus-rain collection, with measured target distance and manually reviewed bounding boxes, is a potentially valuable complement to large but less controlled driving datasets.

PCD attempts to combine localization quality, confidence, and uncertainty rather than reducing performance to a single deterministic cutoff. Evaluating five detector families and reporting both PCD and conventional metrics provides an informative initial case study.
The manuscript communicates the high-level motivation and workflow clearly, and the qualitative plots make the degradation of detection quality with distance easy to understand.
weaknesses: The core statistical formulation contains consequential inconsistencies. Equation 6 computes both sums using f(x_tau), rather than observation-specific fitted values f(x_i), so it is not a likelihood based on the spline residuals described in the text. Equation 7 then applies l to x_tau and x_n although l was defined over an index tau. These issues make the reported change points difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The variance estimator in Equation 9 is the standard deviation of the raw responses within a segment, not of residuals y_i-f(x_i). Because the fitted mean changes substantially with distance, this quantity conflates mean trend with conditional variance and undermines the claimed heteroscedastic uncertainty model.

The algorithm is incomplete at important edge cases: the segment set in Equation 9 omits the intervals before the first and after the last change point and is undefined when there are zero change points, yet Table 2 reports zero change points for clear-weather Deformable DETR while Table 3 still reports its mPCD. The manuscript does not explain the implementation used in such cases.

Equation 10 takes the farthest individual distance satisfying a pointwise probability condition. It therefore does not guarantee reliable detection throughout the range up to that distance, contrary to the paper's repeated 'within which' and 'consistently' interpretations. An isolated far-range crossing or spline fluctuation can determine PCD, making it sensitive to sampling density, trajectory extent, and outliers.

IoU multiplied by detector confidence has no established probabilistic interpretation, and confidence scores are not calibrated or directly comparable across the five architectures, especially between conventional and vision-language detectors. Modeling this bounded, often zero-inflated product with an unvalidated Gaussian distribution can also assign probability outside its valid range. No goodness-of-fit, calibration analysis, or alternative distribution is provided.

The evidence is too limited to establish robustness or added value: there is one target sedan, one apparent trajectory per condition, and only 278/317 temporally correlated frames. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, synthetic checks of change-point recovery, sensitivity analyses for K, lambda, alpha, or threshold grids, or comparisons with simpler distance-binned recall/quality baselines.

The clear and rainy sequences have different distance ranges and distributions, while temporal dependence violates the stated independent-error assumption. Treating sequential frames as independent and recursively testing segments without discussing multiple-testing control further weakens the statistical claims.

The evaluation protocol suppresses all but the highest-scoring 'car' prediction in each image, so it does not assess false positives as an operational detector normally would. The calculation and interpretation of COCO-style mAP and size-specific AP under this protocol are insufficiently specified; several identical AP_M/AP_L values across otherwise different models also warrant explanation.

mPCD is described as both a surface volume and an average, but its integration domain, discretization, normalization, and treatment of strict inequalities/boundaries are not formally specified. Together with fixed unexplained choices K=10 and lambda=0.6, this prevents faithful reproduction.

The dataset and code URLs are blank in the submitted manuscript. Claims that this is the only public controlled dataset and that experiments are 'extensive' are not supported by the narrow single-object, two-condition evaluation. These reproducibility and claim-calibration issues are secondary to the core statistical problems but still significant.

strengths: The controlled clear-versus-rain collection is potentially useful, and precise target distances enable an application-relevant analysis not directly provided by aggregate AP.
The paper clearly motivates range-dependent evaluation, tests five detector families, and exposes the operating thresholds used by PCD.
The presentation is generally understandable, with a useful computation schematic, equations, and threshold-sensitivity plots.
weaknesses: The central probabilistic model is unjustified. IoU times confidence is bounded, has a visible point mass at zero, and combines differently calibrated detector scores, yet it is modeled as Gaussian without calibration or goodness-of-fit testing. Thus P(Y > y_t) lacks a validated reliability interpretation.

PCD takes the maximum sampled distance satisfying a pointwise condition but does not require reliability at every nearer distance. A distant re-crossing can therefore determine PCD despite unreliable gaps, contradicting the claimed farthest distance "within which" detection is consistently reliable.

The change-point method appears incorrectly or ambiguously specified: Equation (6) uses f(x_tau) rather than f(x_i), while Equation (7) inconsistently uses l(tau), l(x_tau), and l(x_n). Recursive testing lacks multiplicity correction, minimum segment lengths, uncertainty intervals, and sensitivity analysis.

The weather comparison is confounded. Each condition contains only one short sequential trajectory of one red sedan, the sequences have different sample counts and distance distributions, and adjacent frames are treated as independent. There are no repeated drives, matched-distance analyses, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests for PCD/mPCD.

The experiments do not demonstrate added value over simpler alternatives such as distance-binned recall, range-stratified AP, empirical detection probability, or a monotone reliability boundary. No downstream FCW/AEB analysis establishes that PCD predicts decision stability or safety.
The claim that static metrics overlook the weather effect is contradicted by Table 3: all conventional aggregate metrics already decline in rain for every detector.

mPCD is underspecified: it is alternately described as a surface volume and a mean, with no precise integration or normalization formula. Its value depends on an arbitrary threshold grid, uncalibrated model scores, distance sampling, and dataset maximum range. Key choices such as K=10, lambda=0.6, alpha, and the Gaussian assumption receive no ablation.

The protocol forces each image to contribute the highest-scoring car box and does not fully specify matching or no-detection handling. A single positive object with no meaningful negative or multi-object cases cannot properly assess false positives. Identical AP_M and AP_L values across several substantially different detectors are unexplained and raise implementation or reporting concerns.

The dataset claims are broader than the evidence: camera, radar, and LiDAR are advertised, but experiments cover only front-camera detection of one red sedan under two daylight conditions. No external dataset or other perception task is evaluated.

Reproducibility is poor: dataset and code URLs are blank, and exact checkpoints, preprocessing, AP implementation, box-selection rules, change-point stopping rules, and an executable mPCD definition are missing.

The range-aware motivation has merit, but the unsupported probability model, inconsistent distance definition, confounded single-run experiment, missing baselines and uncertainty analysis, and incomplete reproducibility undermine the principal reliability and safety claims. These are consequential scientific weaknesses rather than presentation refinements.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical limitation of frame-level detection metrics: they do not directly communicate the distance over which an autonomous-driving perception system remains reliable. PCD is intuitive, has meaningful physical units, and exposes the trade-off between detection quality, reliability probability, and range.

SensorRainFall offers a useful controlled comparison between clear daylight and heavy rain (64 mm/h), with object distance and manually reviewed bounding boxes. Holding the scene largely fixed is valuable for isolating weather effects.

The empirical study includes five substantially different detectors and reports both conventional AP measures and the proposed metric. The threshold-surface visualization is informative, and the observed reductions in mPCD under rain are qualitatively plausible.

The manuscript is generally organized and visually clear, provides several implementation choices such as spline order, knot count, penalty, and significance level, and explicitly acknowledges that evaluation is presently restricted to one dataset and task.
weaknesses: The statistical formulation has consequential correctness concerns. Equation 6 computes residuals using f(x_tau) for every observation rather than f(x_i), and Equation 7 inconsistently passes distances x_tau and x_n to a likelihood defined over indices. Moreover, Equation 9 estimates segment noise as std(y_A), which includes variation of the fitted mean across distance rather than the residual standard deviation. It is unclear whether these are manuscript errors or reflect the implementation, but either interpretation prevents validation of the reported PCD values.

The Gaussian model is poorly matched to the observed variable. IoU times confidence is bounded in [0,1] and the plots show a substantial point mass at zero, pronounced skew, and temporal dependence. No diagnostic, robustness analysis, or alternative bounded/zero-inflated model is provided. Sequentially applying change-point tests also raises multiple-testing and minimum-segment concerns that are not addressed.

PCD is defined as the farthest individual distance satisfying a pointwise probability condition. It therefore need not guarantee reliability at every nearer distance and can select an isolated distant region after intervening failures, contrary to the claimed interpretation of a distance 'within which' detection is consistently reliable. Its value is also capped by the observed distance support, which differs between clear and rainy sequences (214 m versus 241 m), complicating comparisons.

Detector confidence scores are not calibrated probabilities and are not comparable across architectures. Multiplying an uncalibrated score by IoU has no established probabilistic interpretation, yet the paper uses this product to rank heterogeneous models without calibration or sensitivity analysis. The resulting mPCD ranking also closely follows mean IoU-times-confidence, so distinct added information is not convincingly demonstrated.

The evaluation does not establish validity beyond detecting an already obvious weather degradation: every conventional metric in Table 3 also declines under rain. There is no comparison with simpler range-aware baselines such as distance-binned recall, recall-distance AUC, or a thresholded maximum-detection range; no connection to downstream braking safety; and no confidence intervals, bootstrap analysis, repeated traversals, or synthetic recovery experiment showing that the change points are accurate.

The dataset evidence is narrow: 595 temporally correlated frames, one red sedan, one route, two recordings, and two conditions. Clear and rain have different distance distributions, and the acquisition/accuracy of the claimed precise distance ground truth is not described. Although radar and LiDAR are advertised, the reported benchmark and annotations concern only camera bounding boxes. These factors substantially limit the broader dataset and robustness claims.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the exact mPCD averaging/integration formula and normalization are not specified, pretrained checkpoint identifiers and missing-detection handling are unclear, and the text says only the highest-confidence 'car' box is retained, leaving false positives and AP computation ambiguous. Several identical size-specific AP values across different models also merit verification.

The related-work coverage is too limited to substantiate originality claims: it omits substantial literature on confidence calibration, probabilistic detection, adverse-weather robustness, distance-stratified evaluation, and controlled-weather datasets. Smaller presentation issues include overstated terms such as 'statistically significant reliability,' unsupported practical threshold recommendations, and the inaccurate statement that deterministic detector architectures contrast with multimodal models.

strengths: PCD addresses a practically important limitation of aggregate detection metrics by expressing performance as a physically interpretable reliable-detection distance, parameterized by quality and probability requirements.

The controlled SensorRainFall collection is potentially useful: it provides sequential, distance-tagged data under four lighting/weather conditions, with bounding-box and instance-mask annotations for vehicle and pedestrian targets.

The empirical study covers ten established models, both detection and instance segmentation, and reports conventional metrics alongside aPCD. Several examples clearly illustrate that distance-dependent behavior can distinguish models with similar or differently ranked AP.

Including complete benchmark tables, implementation configurations, change-point locations, and synthetic change-point experiments is helpful for analysis and potential reproduction. weaknesses: The probabilistic foundation is not technically justified. IoU multiplied by confidence is bounded, strongly zero-inflated by misses, and visibly non-Gaussian, yet each segment is modeled as Gaussian. Sequential frames are also correlated, contrary to the stated independent-error assumption. Consequently, the estimated exceedance probabilities need not be calibrated probabilities of reliable detection.

PCD is defined as the maximum distance satisfying the probability inequality, which does not guarantee reliability at every shorter distance. A non-monotone spline or isolated distant recovery can therefore produce a large PCD despite intervening failures, contradicting the paper's interpretation as the distance 'within which' detection is consistently reliable. No monotonicity constraint or contiguous-prefix definition resolves this issue.

The change-point formulation appears erroneous or insufficiently specified: Equation 7 uses residuals relative to f(x_tau) rather than f(x_i), and Equation 8 inconsistently applies l to x_tau. Recursive testing is presented without minimum segment lengths or multiple-testing control. The simulations evaluate mainly the number of detected changes under very large variance shifts, not localization error, false-positive rate, coverage, or the downstream error of PCD. These issues materially affect reproducibility and validity.

The claimed advantage over existing metrics is demonstrated through selected ranking disagreements, not validated. There are no comparisons to simple distance-binned recall, range-conditioned AP, survival/quantile models, or threshold-crossing baselines; no correlation with an external safety outcome such as braking or TTC error; and no uncertainty intervals or independent-run analysis. Thus, the evidence does not establish that variance change points or aPCD add reliable information beyond the distance trend in the mean score.

Model confidence is not calibrated and is not comparable across architectures, yet confidence is multiplied by IoU and used directly for cross-model rankings. The manuscript also does not adequately specify treatment of missed detections, multiple predictions, false positives, matching, aPCD integration bounds/grid/normalization, or spline boundary behavior. The procedure of retaining only the highest-confidence prediction for the target class may further hide false alarms.

The dataset evidence is too confounded to support broad robustness or safety claims. It contains only one sedan and one surrogate pedestrian from a single facility, apparently along highly correlated trajectories, without independent repeated runs or held-out validation. Conditions have different sample counts and distance distributions, while the metric itself is distance-dependent. The poncho-induced pedestrian halo and one-lane offset further limit ecological validity.

Important dataset descriptions conflict: the main paper states all rainy conditions use 64 mm/h, whereas the supplement reports two nominal intensities of 20 and 40 mm/h without mapping them to the four evaluated conditions. The paper also advertises camera, radar, and LiDAR data, but the presented benchmark and metric validation use only images. These are substantive reproducibility and scope problems; duplicated sentences, small plots, grammatical errors, and incomplete anonymized links are secondary presentation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical question: conventional aggregate detection metrics do not directly communicate how performance changes with object distance and operating conditions.

PCD has an intuitive physical unit, exposes user-adjustable quality and probability thresholds, and could motivate useful distance-conditioned evaluation if reformulated and validated more rigorously.

The SensorRainFall data provide controlled lighting and rain scenarios, precise target distances, and both box and mask annotations. weaknesses: The central probabilistic interpretation is not technically justified. IoU multiplied by confidence is bounded, heavily zero-inflated, and visibly non-Gaussian, yet it is modeled as normally distributed. Moreover, variation across different sequential frames is called model-output stochasticity, although the inputs, distances, and scene content change. This does not estimate predictive uncertainty at a fixed operating point.

The PCD definition does not guarantee the claimed reliable interval. Equation 2 takes the maximum distance satisfying a pointwise probability condition. Because the fitted spline is not constrained to be monotone, reliability may fail at an intermediate distance and recover later, causing PCD to select an isolated far-distance crossing rather than the boundary within which detection is consistently reliable.

The variance model and change-point derivation contain serious ambiguities. Equation 7 subtracts f(x_tau) from every observation rather than f(x_i), which is inconsistent with the regression model. Errors are assumed independent despite sequential video sampling, recursive hypothesis tests are applied without a stated multiplicity correction or minimum segment length, and a single constant variance is assigned to each potentially broad distance segment.

PCD is not comparable fairly across models without confidence calibration. Detector confidence scales can differ substantially, so multiplying confidence by IoU and applying common thresholds may reward calibration or score scaling rather than perception quality. No calibration procedure or invariance analysis is provided.

The evidence does not validate the paper's main safety and robustness claims. The experiments mostly show that PCD sometimes ranks models differently from AP and then interpret those differences as desirable. There is no external reliability criterion, repeated-run test, downstream braking or collision analysis, correlation with safety outcomes, comparison against simpler distance-binned AP/recall or first-detection-range baselines, or demonstration that PCD predicts failures better than alternatives.

aPCD is insufficiently specified. The manuscript calls it both a volume and an average but does not precisely define the integration domain, normalization, threshold grid, interpolation, or numerical procedure. There are also no sensitivity studies for the spline basis count, lambda, significance level, change points, sampling density, confidence calibration, or threshold-grid resolution.

The dataset cannot support broad robustness conclusions. It contains only two fixed targets on one controlled track, apparently with one or very few sequential passes per condition; distance is therefore confounded with time and trajectory. Conditions also have different sample counts and maximum ranges, which can directly affect a maximum-distance metric. Generalization is not tested on another dataset or natural traffic.

The dataset description is internally inconsistent: the main paper states a rainfall rate of 64 mm/h, whereas the supplement describes two nominal rates of 20 and 40 mm/h. The abstract emphasizes camera, radar, and LiDAR data, but the presented annotations and benchmarks use front-view camera images only. These discrepancies materially impair reproducibility and interpretation.

The change-point simulations are too favorable and incomplete. They use very large variance changes, report mainly the number rather than localization accuracy, false-positive rate, or power, and do not test bounded zero-inflated data resembling IoU times confidence. The claim that an approximately threefold change suffices is also ambiguous because the plotted variable is standard deviation, not variance.

The claim of a safety envelope is substantially overstated. Choosing p and quality thresholds heuristically does not establish a safe operating domain; safety also depends on speed, reaction time, object class, false-positive costs, temporal persistence, planner behavior, and uncertainty in the estimated boundary. Statements recommending threshold ranges for emergency braking or lane keeping are unsupported by experiments.

The related-work discussion omits important adverse-weather and distance-aware driving benchmarks and provides no serious comparison with probabilistic calibration, detection-range, risk-aware, or temporal-stability metrics. Presentation problems—including grammatical errors, duplicated text, an unexplained 'Mask R-CNN ok' table entry, and confusing statements about training despite claiming zero-shot inference—further reduce clarity, although these are secondary to the methodological issues.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of frame-aggregated metrics: they do not directly describe the distance over which an autonomous-driving perception system remains reliable. Reporting performance in meters is operationally interpretable and potentially complementary to AP/AR.

SensorRainFall is a useful controlled-data contribution. It provides synchronized distance measurements and manually annotated boxes and masks for vehicle and pedestrian targets under four weather/illumination settings, enabling comparisons in which some environmental factors are controlled.

The empirical study covers five detectors and five instance-segmentation models, two target types, and four conditions. The complete supplementary tables are helpful, and examples where aPCD and AP rank models differently illustrate the intended complementary perspective.

The paper describes the spline and variance-change-point procedure in substantial detail, reports its principal hyperparameters, and includes synthetic investigations of sample-size and effect-size behavior. Public data and code would further support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central reliability interpretation is not technically established. PCD is the maximum distance at which a pointwise modeled probability passes a threshold; it does not require the criterion to hold at every shorter distance. With a non-monotonic spline or separated successful regions, PCD can therefore label intervening failures as part of a safe operating envelope. No monotonicity constraint, contiguous-range definition, or empirical coverage test is provided.

The statistical model makes strong, largely unvalidated assumptions. Observations from sequential driving frames are treated as independent Gaussian samples, while nearby frames are temporally correlated and there appear to be no repeated independent observations at the same distance. Segment-level residual variation can consequently mix genuine stochastic uncertainty with changes in distance, pose, blur, and temporal conditions. Normality, calibration, goodness of fit, and uncertainty intervals for PCD/aPCD are not evaluated.

IoU multiplied by raw confidence is an ad hoc reliability variable. Confidence scores are not calibrated or directly comparable across model families, and retaining only the highest-scoring car/person prediction ignores additional false positives. Thus a detector producing many unsafe false alarms can receive the same PCD as one producing none. The paper does not compare against simpler distance-aware baselines such as binned recall, recall-versus-distance AUC, maximum range under a recall constraint, or calibrated risk-coverage curves.

Evidence that aPCD captures robustness beyond conventional summaries remains limited to selected qualitative examples. Across the full tables, aPCD appears closely associated with the mean IoU-times-confidence score, but the manuscript provides no correlation analysis, ablation of the variance modeling/change-point component, bootstrap stability analysis, or downstream braking/planning experiment supporting the stronger safety-envelope claims.

Important reproducibility details are missing or inconsistent. The threshold domain, grid, normalization, and numerical integration used to obtain aPCD are not specified. The main paper states a controlled rainfall rate of 64 mm/h, whereas the supplement describes 20 and 40 mm/h, without mapping these intensities to the reported conditions. Equation 7 also appears to compute residuals using f(x_tau) rather than f(x_i), which makes the stated change-point likelihood questionable unless it is a typographical error.

The dataset is narrow—roughly 1,231 frames from one facility, one sedan, and one surrogate pedestrian—and the method is evaluated only on this same controlled dataset. This does not by itself warrant rejection, but combined with the unresolved metric definition and validation issues, it leaves the claimed general utility and safety meaning insufficiently supported. The dataset and operational motivation are worthwhile, yet the consequential weaknesses currently outweigh them.
